data.title: FB Bancorp Reports $515,000 Nine-Month Net Income; Q3 Net Income $466,000
data.description:
FB Bancorp reported net income of $515,000 for the nine months ended September 30, 2026, including $1.7 million from continuing operations and a $1.1 million loss from discontinued operations. Third-quarter net income was $466,000, all from continuing operations. Continuing-operations diluted earnings per share were $0.11 for the nine-month period and $0.03 for the quarter.

Financial Highlights

  • Nine-month net interest income was $35.9 million, compared with $36.2 million in the same 2025 period; third-quarter net interest income was $12.1 million, versus $12.3 million.
  • Total non-interest income was $4.4 million for the first nine months, up from $3.1 million a year earlier. The period included $1.2 million in proceeds from bank-owned life insurance.
  • Total non-interest expenses rose to $37.1 million for the nine months, from $33.8 million. Third-quarter expenses were $12.1 million, compared with $11.7 million.
  • Nine-month net income was $515,000, compared with $2.7 million in 2025; net income from continuing operations was $1.7 million, versus $3.4 million. Third-quarter net income was $466,000, compared with $1.1 million.
  • Basic and diluted earnings per share from continuing operations were $0.11 for the nine months and $0.03 for the quarter. Total basic and diluted earnings per share were $0.03 for the nine-month period.

Business Highlights

  • The sale of substantially all assets and liabilities of the NOLA Lending Group mortgage banking segment closed on March 1, 2026. The segment had no material operating activity in the third quarter, and the company does not expect material future activity or losses from it.
  • At September 30, the bank operated 18 locations and had 199 full-time equivalent employees. The mortgage segment’s exit reduced staffing by approximately 108 employees.
  • Commercial loans increased during the first nine months, while residential mortgage loans ran off; the company expects continued runoff of residential mortgages.
  • Following additional information about a borrower’s expected payment performance, management classified a commercial loan with an approximately $19.8 million principal balance as substandard at September 30. The company ordered an updated appraisal after learning of a new lease agreement related to the collateral.

data.title: Lululemon Appoints Two Key Executives Amid Leadership Shakeup
data.description:
By Natalie Weger

Lululemon Athletica appointed two new key executives as Chief Executive Heidi O'Neill rounds out her leadership team to help address slumping sales at the athleisure company.

The company on Friday said it has appointed Ben Hallam as chief brand officer and Emily Sunderland as chief strategy officer, effective Nov. 9 and Nov. 23, respectively

Hallam, who succeeds Nikki Neuburger, most recently served as the senior vice president of marketing at Four Seasons Hotels and Resorts.

Sunderland was a managing director and partner at Boston Consulting Group, succeeding Rachel Acheson.

O'Neill, a former Nike executive, has already made several executive changes since she took the helm of the company in September. Last month, she brought on the former head of Gap's Athleta brand as president and chief product officer, and also tapped a former Walmart executive as chief operating officer.

Lululemon said it's still looking for a chief technology officer and chief communications officer.

Write to Natalie Weger at natalie.weger@wsj.com.

data.title: IPOs Struggle in Tech Selloff. Berkshire Has a Winner. — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Andrew Bary

The old investment adage to avoid initial public offerings has held up this year, as many stocks are trading well below their IPO prices.

Barron's looked at 18 companies that made their U.S. stock-market debuts in 2026, including marquee offerings like SpaceX, Cerebras Systems, Innio, Madison Air Solutions and Jersey Mike's, found that 15 of them are below their offering prices. Many are down 50% or more.

SK Hynix, already public in South Korea, made its U.S. debut in July through an offering of American depositary shares. That stock also is trading below its U.S. offering price in July.

Why do IPOs often falter? Companies that come public often are in hot industries, and carry high valuations to reflect investor optimism. That enthusiasm often wanes, however. This year, some deals were keyed off the AI buildout and enthusiasm for that trend has faded.

There are some winners, notably Arxis, a defense contractor with an aerospace focus; Pershing Square, Bill Ackman's investment management company, and Bending Spoons, the rollup of mature tech companies like AOL.

Give Berkshire Hathaway some credit. The company headed now by CEO Greg Abel picked the right deal when it invested $600 million in Bending Spoons at the July IPO at $29 a share. The stock traded recently at $45, up 55%. In October, Berkshire bought another $330 million of stock at $33.

Berkshire rarely buys IPOs — reflecting former CEO Warren Buffett's well-founded aversion to them. It participated in Snowflake's IPO in 2020.

Looking at some of the larger deals, SpaceX trades around $131, against an IPO price of $135; Cerebras at $82, less than half its IPO price of $185; and SK Hynix at $124, versus its U.S. offering price of $149.

One of the better ways to play IPOs in a diversified way is through the Renaissance IPO ETF. It adds newly public companies every three months as part of a regular rebalancing and companies cycle out after three years. Individual holdings are capped at a 10% weighting at rebalancing.

Its largest holdings now are SpaceX at nearly 10%, followed by SK Hynix and Astera Labs, both at more than 7%. The ETF, now around $45, is off about 2% so far this year.

Be careful about SK Hynix ADRs. While chip stocks have come under pressure, SK Hynix's U.S. shares trade at a big premium to the Korean shares that Barron's estimates is close to 50%.

Busted IPOs also can be a good place to look for values, and there are many companies to comb through this year.

Write to Andrew Bary at andrew.bary@barrons.com

data.title: Nasdaq rebounds but posts fourth straight weekly decline
data.description:
Key points:
  • Indexes: Dow slips, Nasdaq, S&P gain
  • Tech stocks bounce back from worst day in more than a year
  • October jobs report surprises to the upside

By Colin Barr and Shashwat Chauhan

Technology stocks bounced back on Friday from their worst drubbing in more than a year, but the Nasdaq Composite Index posted a fourth consecutive weekly decline as investors sifted for clues about what comes next in the AI trade.

Gains within technology were broadly shared, with the semiconductor index rallying 4.2%. Nvidia rose 2.8%, Advanced Micro Devices added 11% and Sandisk rebounded almost 4%. Shares within the sector opened strongly and held much of their gains, with the Nasdaq ending up 1.1% after trading as much as 2% higher.

The broad revival underscores investor faith in the AI buildout that has driven US stock indexes to dozens of record closes this year, despite a shakeout that began with a US long-term Treasury yield spike in August and the stock volatility of the past month.

“We still think AI is the dominant theme in this bull market,” said Keith Lerner, chief investment officer at Truist Advisory Services in Atlanta. “We are still giving technology the benefit of the doubt.”

The S&P 500 climbed 23 points, or 0.32%, to end the session at 7,376.86 points. The Nasdaq gained 264 points to 24,579.43 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average declined 237 points, or 0.46%, to 51,285.73 points.

Lerner said he views the selloff this week, which has taken the Nasdaq into correction territory denoting a 10% decline from its peak a month ago, as likely offering a longer-term buying opportunity for many investors. For the week, the Nasdaq declined 3.4%, the S&P dropped 2.7% and the Dow slipped 0.9%.

“AI has gone on trial several times in this cycle and come away with an innocent verdict,” said Adam Turnquist, chief cross-asset strategist for LPL Financial in Charlotte, North Carolina. Referring to the US midterm election results that spurred heavy selling in AI stocks, he said, “This week we saw a little bit of a knee-jerk reaction.”

The S&P 500 sectors were mixed, with information technology leading gains and consumer staples and healthcare lagging. The benchmark index had its worst week in more than a year.

US nonfarm payrolls increased more than expected in October and the unemployment rate fell to 4.1%, suggesting the labor market remained resilient. Traders added to bets that the Federal Reserve could hike rates as soon as next month, with a 78% chance of a December move compared with a 70% chance seen earlier, according to LSEG.

"Those are strong numbers,” said Joe Saluzzi, co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey. But he asked, “Will the Fed want to raise interest rates in the face of a market which is teetering?"

Tesla rose 4.2% and SpaceX jumped 8.6% among technology shares bouncing back from Thursday’s plunge. Among other stock movers, software firm Atlassian dropped 16% after reporting first-quarter results. Airbnb climbed 12% after the vacation rental platform raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth forecast.

Oil prices were slightly lower, adding to bullish sentiment for riskier assets, and were on track for sharp weekly declines. The S&P 500 energy index dropped 12% for the week, its worst performance since April 2025.

Despite the volatility, Turnquist said a bullish sign for the AI buildout is the performance of copper, a major ingredient in data centers and other technology. Copper futures remain above their 200-day moving average and their September lows, he said.

“If this is real demand destruction on AI, you’d think copper would start to roll over,” Turnquist said. “It’s not a perfect barometer, but I look at it as a reality check.”

data.title: Hawaiian Electric Profit, Sales Rise After American Savings Bank Sale
data.description:
By Katherine Hamilton

Hawaiian Electric Industries logged higher profit and revenue in the third quarter, thanks in large part to selling a portion of its stake in American Savings Bank.

The utilities company posted a profit of $35 million, or 20 cents a share, compared with $31 million, or 18 cents a share, a year earlier.

Stripping out certain one-time items, such as those related to the Maui wildfire, adjusted per-share earnings were 13 cents a share.

Revenue rose 28% to $1.01 billion.

Hawaiian Electric's holding and other companies, which includes non-utility businesses, swung to a profit of $22 million, from a loss of $6 million. That primarily reflected pre-tax gains on the sale of American Savings Bank shares.

Hawaiian Electric sold 35% of its 9.9% stake in the bank's initial public offering, which was in September. Its remaining stake is about 6.4%.

Within the company's core business profit fell to $13 million from $37 million, mainly due to higher costs.

Operations and management expenses were higher than the year before, mostly due to storm costs in August and September.

data.title: Robust Hiring Defied Expectations in October, With 165,000 New Jobs — WSJ
data.description:
By Justin Lahart

The U.S. added 165,000 jobs in October, in a sign that the labor market could be strengthening.

The numbers

Friday's report from the Labor Department topped economists' expectations for a 59,000 job gain. The unemployment rate, meanwhile, slipped to 4.1%, lower than expectations for 4.2%.

Jobs figures for both September and August were revised higher by a combined 84,000. That is a strong indication that the job market has pulled out of its midyear doldrums. The economy has added an average of 137,000 jobs a month over the past three months.

"It's as good as can be, really," said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon.

Daco said that the drop in the unemployment rate was especially notable given that the labor-force participation rate — the share of the working-age population either working or looking for work — picked up last month. That is an indication that more people were entering the labor market and finding jobs.

Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo, pointed out that the unemployment rate has now been under 5% for roughly five years. That puts it just short of a record 64-month stretch from 1965 to 1970.

Where jobs were gained and lost

October's employment growth was driven by an increase of 70,000 professional and business-services jobs — well above the average monthly gain of 15,000 over the previous 12 months.

That could be a sign that artificial intelligence isn't yet sapping white-collar jobs to the degree some people fear.

The finance sector — one area seen as heavily exposed to AI — added 7,000 jobs, but has been in a weakening trend. And the information sector shed 1,000 jobs.

Elsewhere, the AI build-out has for some time been fueling jobs for workers who are building data centers.

Construction overall shed 3,000 jobs. On a more granular level, however, the report showed that employers last month hired almost 8,000 nonresidential specialty-trade contractors, workers such as electricians who are in high demand at data-center sites.

At the same time, employers shed more than 15,000 such residential roles, a sign of how higher interest rates are slowing housing construction.

Manufacturing added 19,000 jobs, bolstered by gains in computer and electronic-product machinery and primary metal manufacturing. All of those sectors are seen as beneficiaries of the AI build-out.

What AI means for the jobs market

On balance, Samuel Tombs, chief U.S. economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, reckons that gains from AI in areas like manufacturing aren't enough to completely offset losses elsewhere.

"I think AI is a modest drag, but it is not a dramatically deteriorating picture," he said.

Healthcare was a continued source of employment growth, adding 42,000 jobs.

Tombs also thinks that the renewed strength in the jobs report in part reflects what has been a strong stock market — Thursday's meltdown aside — and a relatively easy financing environment for companies. The volatility that financial markets have recently experienced could change that.

Wages

Average hourly earnings were up 3.1% from a year earlier. That likely marked the seventh month in a row where earnings growth fell short of inflation.

But from a month earlier, hourly earnings were up a robust 0.4%. That was in part from the broadening in job growth into areas with better pay, such as professional and business services.

How markets reacted

Stocks rose following the report, taking back some of the ground they lost in Thursday's sharp, AI-driven selloff. Treasury yields were little changed, however, while futures markets continued to signal an expectation that Federal Reserve policymakers will likely raise rates when they next meet in December.

What this means for the Fed

Fed policymakers right now are more focused on inflation, which has remained firmly above their 2% target, than on the job market, which has remained sturdy despite some weakness earlier this year.

Officials will have one additional month of jobs data to parse by the time they gather for their next meeting. They will also be watching closely to see if this week's market turmoil turns into a sustained selloff. That means that Friday's jobs numbers could become just a footnote by the time they gather in December.

Midterm postmortem

Dissatisfaction with the job market — and the economy overall — might have been a factor in Democrats' victory over Republicans in this week's midterm elections.

One reason is that wages have struggled to keep up with inflation. That means that, even as the economy has powered ahead, a smaller and smaller share of economic growth has gone directly to workers. On Thursday, the Labor Department reported that the share of nonfarm business output accruing to workers' compensation fell to 53% in the third quarter — the lowest level in 80 years of data.

Another issue is that while layoffs have been low, so has the pace of hiring. That has made it difficult for people trying to break into the job market, such as new graduates. The low-hire market has also made it harder for people to switch jobs — one of the main ways for workers to get pay jumps.
